title: Meister Pfriem
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 178. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved (daß, gieng, thun, wußte, ward).
about: A restless, fault-finding little cobbler — a Pfriem is the shoemaker’s awl he never puts down — is swept up in a dream-vision of Heaven, where he cannot stop correcting the workmanship of the angels themselves until he is thrown out. It is a gentle satire on the compulsive know-it-all: no one is harmed, and Pfriem wakes chastened rather than punished. His pockmarked face and darting eyes are drawn with real relish in the opening lines.

sentences.t: Meister Pfriem war ein kleiner hagerer aber lebhafter Mann, der keinen Augenblick Ruhe hatte.
sentences.l: Master Pfriem was a small, spare, but lively man, who had not a moment’s rest.
sentences.i: Master Pfriem was a little, lean, but lively man who never had a moment’s peace.
sentences.n: A Pfriem is the shoemaker’s awl, the pointed tool that pricks the holes for the thread; the man is named after the sharpest thing in his shop, and the name is left standing in the German. “hager” — gaunt, spare.

sentences.t: Sein Gesicht, aus dem nur die aufgestülpte Nase vorragte, war pockennarbig und leichenblaß, sein Haar grau und struppig, seine Augen klein, aber sie blitzten unaufhörlich rechts und links hin.
sentences.l: His face, out of which only the turned-up nose jutted forward, was pock-marked and corpse-pale, his hair grey and shaggy, his eyes small, but they flashed ceaselessly to right and left.
sentences.i: His face, from which nothing stood out but the turned-up nose, was pock-marked and deathly pale, his hair grey and unkempt, his eyes small — but they darted ceaselessly right and left.
sentences.n: German lets the verb drop through a list of descriptions: “sein Haar grau und struppig” has no was, it is simply carried over from the first clause. “leichenblaß” is literally corpse-pale; “pockennarbig”, scarred by smallpox. “grau” here is plain High German grey.

sentences.t: Er bemerkte alles, tadelte alles, wußte alles besser und hatte in allem Recht.
sentences.l: He noticed everything, found fault with everything, knew everything better and was right in everything.
sentences.i: He noticed everything, found fault with everything, knew better than anyone, and was right about it all.
sentences.n: “Recht haben” — to be right; German uses the noun Recht, ‘the right’, with haben where English uses an adjective. “alles besser wissen” is the standing phrase for a know-all.

sentences.t: Gieng er auf der Straße, so ruderte er heftig mit beiden Armen, und einmal schlug er einem Mädchen, das Wasser trug, den Eimer so hoch in die Luft, daß er selbst davon begossen ward.
sentences.l: Did he go along the street, then he rowed violently with both arms, and once he struck a girl who was carrying water the pail so high into the air that he himself was doused by it.
sentences.i: If he walked along the street, he would row away with both arms, and once he knocked a water-carrying girl’s pail so high into the air that he was drenched by it himself.
sentences.n: “Gieng er …, so …” is a conditional without wenn: putting the verb first makes the clause mean ‘if, whenever he went’. Three more of these follow. The dative “einem Mädchen” marks whose pail it was — German says ‘struck to a girl the pail’.

sentences.t: „Schafskopf,“ rief er ihr zu indem er sich schüttelte, „konntest du nicht sehen daß ich hinter dir herkam?“
sentences.l: “Sheep’s-head,” he called across to her while he shook himself, “could you not see that I was coming along behind you?”
sentences.i: “Blockhead,” he called out to her as he shook himself, “could you not see that I was coming along behind you?”
sentences.n: “indem” here is the older ‘while, just as’, not the modern ‘by doing’. “zurufen” is separable: rief … zu. The blame lands on the girl he drenched himself with — the whole tale in one exchange.

sentences.t: Seines Handwerks war er ein Schuster, und wenn er arbeitete, so fuhr er mit dem Draht so gewaltig aus, daß er jedem, der sich nicht weit genug in der Ferne hielt, die Faust in den Leib stieß.
sentences.l: Of his trade he was a shoemaker, and when he worked, he drove out with the thread so mightily that he thrust his fist into the body of anyone who did not keep himself far enough off.
sentences.i: By trade he was a cobbler, and when he worked he pulled the thread through with such a sweep that he drove his fist into the body of anyone who did not keep well clear.
sentences.n: “Seines Handwerks” is a genitive of respect: as to his trade. The Draht is the cobbler’s waxed thread, drawn through the awl-holes with a long pull of the whole arm — “ausfahren” is that sweeping movement outward.

sentences.t: Kein Geselle blieb länger als einen Monat bei ihm, denn er hatte an der besten Arbeit immer etwas auszusetzen.
sentences.l: No journeyman stayed longer than a month with him, for he always had something to find fault with in the best work.
sentences.i: No journeyman stayed with him longer than a month, for he always had something to criticize in the very best work.
sentences.n: “an etwas auszusetzen haben” — to have something to object to in a thing. A Geselle is a journeyman: trained, but not yet a master with a shop of his own.

sentences.t: Bald waren die Stiche nicht gleich, bald war ein Schuh länger, bald ein Absatz höher als der andere, bald war das Leder nicht hinlänglich geschlagen.
sentences.l: Now the stitches were not even, now one shoe was longer, now one heel higher than the other, now the leather was not sufficiently beaten.
sentences.i: One time the stitches were not even, another time one shoe was longer, or one heel higher than the other, or the leather had not been beaten enough.
sentences.n: “bald … bald …” = now … now …, one time … another. Sole-leather was hammered on a stone to compact it before it was cut and sewn, and leather left unbeaten wore through quickly. “Absatz” is the heel of the shoe, not the word’s commoner modern senses.

sentences.t: „Warte“ sagte er zu dem Lehrjungen, „ich will dir schon zeigen wie man die Haut weich schlägt,“ holte den Riemen und gab ihm ein paar Hiebe über den Rücken.
sentences.l: “Wait,” said he to the apprentice, “I will show you all right how one beats the hide soft,” fetched the strap and gave him a couple of blows over the back.
sentences.i: “Just wait,” he said to the apprentice, “I shall show you how a hide is beaten soft,” and he fetched the strap and gave him a few strokes across the back.
sentences.n: The threat turns on a double sense: “die Haut weich schlagen” is what the cobbler does to leather, and it is now what he does to the boy. Nothing is softened here — the beating is on the page.

sentences.t: Faullenzer nannte er sie alle.
sentences.l: Idlers he called them all.
sentences.i: Idlers he called them, every one.
sentences.n: The object stands first for emphasis, a move English can copy here. “Faullenzer” (modern Faulenzer) belongs to faul, lazy.

sentences.t: Er selber brachte aber doch nicht viel vor sich, weil er keine Viertelstunde ruhig sitzen blieb.
sentences.l: He himself, however, brought not much before him, because he did not stay sitting quietly for a quarter of an hour.
sentences.i: Yet he himself got little enough done, because he never stayed sitting quietly for a quarter of an hour together.
sentences.n: “etwas vor sich bringen” is an old idiom for getting work forward, finishing something; the modern phrase would be etwas zustande bringen.

sentences.t: War seine Frau frühmorgens aufgestanden und hatte Feuer angezündet, so sprang er aus dem Bett und lief mit bloßen Füßen in die Küche.
sentences.l: Had his wife got up early in the morning and lit a fire, then he sprang out of bed and ran with bare feet into the kitchen.
sentences.i: If his wife had got up early and lit the fire, he would spring out of bed and run barefoot into the kitchen.
sentences.n: The verb-first conditional again, this time in the pluperfect: “War … aufgestanden und hatte … angezündet” = whenever she had got up and lit the fire.

sentences.t: „Wollt ihr mir das Haus anzünden?“ schrie er, „das ist ja ein Feuer, daß man einen Ochsen dabei braten könnte!
sentences.l: “Do you want to set the house alight on me?” he shouted, “that is a fire such that one could roast an ox at it!
sentences.i: “Do you mean to burn the house down on me?” he shouted. “That is a fire you could roast an ox at!
sentences.n: The dative “mir” is not ‘to me’ but the dative of interest: the burning would be done to my cost. “ja” is a particle of indignant obviousness here and has nothing to do with ‘yes’.

sentences.t: oder kostet das Holz etwa kein Geld?“
sentences.l: or does the wood perhaps cost no money?
sentences.i: or does firewood cost nothing, then?
sentences.n: “etwa” in a question sharpens it into a sneer — ‘or is it that …?’ The lower-case start after the exclamation mark is 1857 practice: the same speech simply runs on.

sentences.t: Standen die Mägde am Waschfaß, lachten und erzählten sich was sie wußten, so schalt er sie aus, „da stehen die Gänse und schnattern und vergessen über dem Geschwätz ihre Arbeit.
sentences.l: Stood the maids at the wash-tub, laughed and told one another what they knew, then he scolded them out: “there stand the geese and cackle and forget their work over the gossip.
sentences.i: If the maids stood at the wash-tub, laughing and telling one another what they knew, he would scold them: “There stand the geese, cackling, and forgetting their work in the gossip.
sentences.n: The third verb-first conditional in a row — the tale builds his whole day out of them. “ausschelten” is separable: schalt … aus. “über dem Geschwätz” — over, that is in the course of, the chatter.

sentences.t: Und wozu die frische Seife?
sentences.l: And what for the fresh soap?
sentences.i: And what is the new soap for?
sentences.n: A question with no verb at all: “wozu” carries it alone, and English has to supply ‘is … for’. “frisch” here means newly cut or newly opened, not clean.

sentences.t: heillose Verschwendung und obendrein eine schändliche Faulheit: sie wollen die Hände schonen und das Zeug nicht ordentlich reiben.“
sentences.l: unholy waste and on top of that a shameful laziness: they want to spare their hands and not rub the stuff properly.
sentences.i: Sheer waste, and shameful idleness on top of it: they want to spare their hands and not scrub the linen properly.
sentences.n: “heillos” is literally ‘without salvation’ and works as an intensifier: unholy, appalling. “das Zeug” is the wash — the cloth and linen in the tub.

sentences.t: Er sprang fort, stieß aber einen Eimer voll Lauge um, so daß die ganze Küche überschwemmt ward.
sentences.l: He sprang away, but knocked over a pail full of lye, so that the whole kitchen was flooded.
sentences.i: He sprang off, but knocked over a pail of lye, so that the whole kitchen was swimming.
sentences.n: “umstoßen” is separable: stieß … um. Lauge is lye, the caustic wash made from wood ash and the ordinary cleaning agent before soap was cheap — his complaint about the soap is answered by his own accident.

sentences.t: Richtete man ein neues Haus auf, so lief er ans Fenster und sah zu.
sentences.l: Did one put up a new house, then he ran to the window and looked on.
sentences.i: If a new house was being put up, he would run to the window and watch.
sentences.n: “aufrichten” (richtete … auf) is used of raising the frame of a building. The impersonal “man” — one, people — turns most naturally into an English passive.

sentences.t: „Da vermauern sie wieder den rothen Sandstein,“ rief er, „der niemals austrocknet; in dem Haus bleibt kein Mensch gesund.
sentences.l: “There they are walling in the red sandstone again,” he cried, “which never dries out; in that house no person stays healthy.
sentences.i: “There they are building the red sandstone in again,” he cried, “and it never dries out; nobody will keep well in that house.
sentences.n: Red sandstone holds damp: a real builder’s objection, and the one grain of sense in the tirade. “vermauern” is to build a thing into a wall.

sentences.t: Und seht einmal wie schlecht die Gesellen die Steine aufsetzen.
sentences.l: And just look how badly the journeymen set the stones up.
sentences.i: And just look how badly the journeymen are laying the stones.
sentences.n: “einmal” after an imperative is not ‘once’ but the small softener ‘just’ — seht einmal, just look.

sentences.t: Der Mörtel taugt auch nichts: Kies muß hinein, nicht Sand.
sentences.l: The mortar is good for nothing either: gravel must go in, not sand.
sentences.i: The mortar is no good either: gravel should go into it, not sand.
sentences.n: “Kies muß hinein” has no verb of motion — German lets the direction word carry it, ‘must (go) in’. Whether Kies here means gravel proper or the coarse sharp grit a mason would call for is not certain; either way he is prescribing the rougher stuff.

sentences.t: Ich erlebe noch daß den Leuten das Haus über dem Kopf zusammenfällt.“
sentences.l: I shall yet live to see that the house falls in over the people’s head.
sentences.i: I shall live to see the house come down over their heads yet.
sentences.n: “erleben” — to live to see. The dative “den Leuten” marks the people it happens to: German says ‘falls to the people the house over the head’.

sentences.t: Er setzte sich und that ein paar Stiche, dann sprang er wieder auf, hakte sein Schurzfell los und rief „ich will nur hinaus und den Menschen ins Gewissen reden.“
sentences.l: He sat himself down and did a couple of stitches, then he sprang up again, unhooked his leather apron and cried “I will just out and speak to people’s conscience.”
sentences.i: He sat down and did a few stitches, then sprang up again, unhooked his leather apron, and cried: “I must just go out and give people a talking-to.”
sentences.n: “jemandem ins Gewissen reden” — to speak to someone’s conscience, to take them seriously to task. “that” is the 1857 spelling of tat (thun = modern tun). “ich will nur hinaus” has no verb of motion once more: ‘I want just out’.

sentences.t: Er gerieth aber an die Zimmerleute.
sentences.l: But he came upon the carpenters.
sentences.i: But it was the carpenters he fell in with.
sentences.n: “an jemanden gerathen” — to fall in with someone, usually to one’s cost; 1857 spells it with -th- (modern geraten).

sentences.t: „Was ist das?“ rief er, „ihr haut ja nicht nach der Schnur.
sentences.l: “What is that?” he cried, “you are not hewing to the line.
sentences.i: “What is this?” he cried. “You are not hewing to the line.
sentences.n: “haut” here is the verb hauen, to hew — not die Haut, the hide, which stood a few sentences back. The Schnur is the chalked cord a carpenter snaps against a timber to mark a straight cut; it is the word for cord or line, and quite separate from the old word Schnur meaning daughter-in-law.

sentences.t: Meint ihr die Balken würden gerad stehen? es weicht einmal alles aus den Fugen.“
sentences.l: Do you think the beams will stand straight? one day everything gives way out of the joints.
sentences.i: Do you suppose the beams will stand straight? One day the whole thing will spring its joints.
sentences.n: “würden … stehen” is the subjunctive of what he doubts. “einmal” here means ‘one day, sooner or later’, and “aus den Fugen weichen” is to come apart at the joints — the phrase behind English ‘out of joint’.

sentences.t: Er riß einem Zimmermann die Axt aus der Hand und wollte ihm zeigen wie er hauen müßte, als aber ein mit Lehm beladener Wagen herangefahren kam, warf er die Axt weg und sprang zu dem Bauer, der neben her gieng.
sentences.l: He tore the axe out of a carpenter’s hand and wanted to show him how he ought to hew; but when a cart loaded with clay came driving up, he threw the axe away and sprang over to the peasant who was walking alongside.
sentences.i: He tore the axe out of a carpenter’s hand and would show him how he ought to hew; but when a cart loaded with clay came driving up, he flung the axe away and sprang across to the peasant walking beside it.
sentences.n: “einem Zimmermann … aus der Hand” is the dative of possession: out of a carpenter’s hand. “kam herangefahren” — came driving up; German joins the motion and the arrival in one phrase.

sentences.t: „Ihr seid nicht recht bei Trost,“ rief er, „wer spannt junge Pferde vor einen schwer beladenen Wagen?
sentences.l: “You are not right in your senses,” he cried, “who harnesses young horses in front of a heavily loaded cart?
sentences.i: “You are out of your wits,” he cried. “Who puts young horses in front of a heavily loaded cart?
sentences.n: “nicht recht bei Trost sein” — not to be in one’s right mind; Trost is otherwise ‘comfort’, and the idiom preserves an old sense of it. “vorspannen” (spannt … vor) is to harness in front — the particle carries the sense, and the whole dream will turn on it.

sentences.t: die armen Thiere werden euch auf dem Platz umfallen.“
sentences.l: the poor beasts will fall down on you on the spot.
sentences.i: the poor beasts will drop where they stand.
sentences.n: “euch” is another dative of interest — they will fall to your cost. “auf dem Platz” = on the spot, where they stand.

sentences.t: Der Bauer gab ihm keine Antwort, und Pfriem lief vor Ärger in seine Werkstätte zurück.
sentences.l: The peasant gave him no answer, and Pfriem ran back into his workshop out of vexation.
sentences.i: The peasant gave him no answer, and Pfriem ran back into his workshop in a rage.
sentences.n: “vor Ärger” — out of vexation; vor with a feeling names the cause of an action.

sentences.t: Als er sich wieder zur Arbeit setzen wollte, reichte ihm der Lehrjunge einen Schuh.
sentences.l: When he wanted to sit himself down to work again, the apprentice handed him a shoe.
sentences.i: When he was about to sit down to work again, the apprentice handed him a shoe.
sentences.n: “wollte” often means ‘was about to’ rather than ‘wanted to’; the sense here is that he was just settling to the bench.

sentences.t: „Was ist das wieder?“ schrie er ihn an, „habe ich euch nicht gesagt ihr solltet die Schuhe nicht so weit ausschneiden?
sentences.l: “What is that again?” he screamed at him, “have I not told you you should not cut the shoes out so wide?
sentences.i: “Now what is this?” he screamed at him. “Have I not told you not to cut the shoes away so far?
sentences.n: “anschreien” — to scream at someone; separable, schrie … an. He uses the plural ihr to a single apprentice, as a master addressed his household. “ausschneiden” of leather is to cut the upper away in shaping it.

sentences.t: wer wird einen solchen Schuh kaufen an dem fast nichts ist als die Sohle?
sentences.l: who will buy such a shoe on which there is almost nothing but the sole?
sentences.i: Who will buy a shoe with almost nothing to it but the sole?
sentences.n: “an dem … ist” — the relative pronoun carries its preposition an, ‘on which there is’. When the upper has been cut too far away, the sole is all that is left.

sentences.t: ich verlange daß meine Befehle unmangelhaft befolgt werden.“
sentences.l: I demand that my orders be followed without defect.
sentences.i: I require my orders to be carried out without a fault.
sentences.n: “unmangelhaft” is literally ‘not-deficiently’: a heavy formal word that sits oddly in a cobbler’s shop, and the pomp is the joke.

sentences.t: „Meister,“ antwortete der Lehrjunge, „ihr mögt wohl Recht haben, daß der Schuh nichts taugt, aber es ist derselbe, den ihr zugeschnitten und selbst in Arbeit genommen habt.
sentences.l: “Master,” answered the apprentice, “you may well be right that the shoe is good for nothing, but it is the same one that you cut out and took into work yourself.
sentences.i: “Master,” answered the apprentice, “you may well be right that the shoe is no good; but it is the very one you cut out and took in hand yourself.
sentences.n: “mögt” is the plain present of mögen, ‘you may’ — the respectful plural again, answering his own ihr. “in Arbeit nehmen” is the shop phrase for taking a piece onto the bench.

sentences.t: Als ihr vorhin aufgesprungen seid, habt ihr ihn vom Tisch herabgeworfen, und ich habe ihn nur aufgehoben.
sentences.l: When you sprang up just now, you threw it down from the table, and I have only picked it up.
sentences.i: When you sprang up just now, you knocked it off the table, and I only picked it up.
sentences.n: “vorhin” — a little while ago, just now. “aufheben” here is simply to pick a thing up off the floor.

sentences.t: Euch könnte es aber ein Engel vom Himmel nicht recht machen.“
sentences.l: But for you an angel from heaven could not do it right.
sentences.i: But an angel from heaven could not do it right for you.
sentences.n: “es jemandem recht machen” — to do a thing to someone’s satisfaction. The apprentice’s line sets up everything that follows: heaven itself will not satisfy him.

sentences.t: Meister Pfriem träumte in einer Nacht er wäre gestorben und befände sich auf dem Weg nach dem Himmel.
sentences.l: Master Pfriem dreamed one night that he had died and found himself on the way to heaven.
sentences.i: One night Master Pfriem dreamed that he had died and was on his way to heaven.
sentences.n: “wäre” and “befände” are subjunctives of reported content: the whole dream is marked as reported, without German needing a word for ‘that’.

sentences.t: Als er anlangte, klopfte er heftig an die Pforte: „es wundert mich,“ sprach er, „daß sie nicht einen Ring am Thor haben, man klopft sich die Knöchel wund.“
sentences.l: When he arrived, he knocked violently at the gate: “it surprises me,” spoke he, “that they do not have a ring on the gate, one knocks one’s knuckles sore.”
sentences.i: When he arrived he knocked violently at the gate. “It surprises me,” he said, “that they have no ring on the door — a man knocks his knuckles raw.”
sentences.n: The Ring is the iron knocker-ring hung on a door. “man klopft sich die Knöchel wund” — the reflexive dative sich marks whose knuckles suffer, and the whole complaint is that heaven is badly fitted out.

sentences.t: Der Apostel Petrus öffnete und wollte sehen wer so ungestüm Einlaß begehrte.
sentences.l: The apostle Peter opened and wanted to see who was demanding admittance so impetuously.
sentences.i: The apostle Peter opened, wanting to see who was demanding admittance so violently.
sentences.n: “ungestüm” is an adverb here, impetuously. “Einlaß begehren” is the formal phrase for asking to be let in — the diction is faintly official, as befits a gate with a porter.

sentences.t: „Ach, ihr seids, Meister Pfriem,“ sagte er, „ich will euch wohl einlassen, aber ich warne euch daß ihr von eurer Gewohnheit ablaßt und nichts tadelt, was ihr im Himmel seht: es könnte euch übel bekommen.“
sentences.l: “Ah, it is you, Master Pfriem,” said he, “I will gladly let you in, but I warn you that you leave off your habit and find fault with nothing that you see in heaven: it could turn out ill for you.”
sentences.i: “Ah, it is you, Master Pfriem,” he said. “I am willing enough to let you in, but I warn you to give up your habit and find fault with nothing you see in heaven: it might go badly for you.”
sentences.n: “seids” = seid es, literally ‘(you) are it’ — German answers a door in that order. “ablassen von” is to leave off, desist from. “übel bekommen” takes a dative: to disagree with someone, to turn out badly for them.

sentences.t: „Ihr hättet euch die Ermahnung sparen können,“ erwiederte Pfriem, „ich weiß schon was sich ziemt, und hier ist, Gott sei Dank, alles vollkommen und nichts zu tadeln, wie auf Erden.“
sentences.l: “You could have spared yourself the admonition,” replied Pfriem, “I know well enough what is seemly, and here, God be thanked, everything is perfect and nothing to find fault with, as on earth.”
sentences.i: “You might have spared yourself the warning,” replied Pfriem. “I know well enough what is fitting, and here, God be thanked, everything is perfect and there is nothing to find fault with, as there is on earth.”
sentences.n: “weiß” is the verb wissen, ‘I know’, and not the adjective weiß, ‘white’ — a trap for the eye. “was sich ziemt” — what is seemly. The last three words, “wie auf Erden”, quietly turn the compliment into a complaint about earth.

sentences.t: Er trat also ein und gieng in den weiten Räumen des Himmels auf und ab.
sentences.l: So he stepped in and went up and down in the wide spaces of heaven.
sentences.i: So he stepped in, and walked up and down in the wide halls of heaven.
sentences.n: “Räumen” is the dative plural of der Raum, space or room — not the verb räumen, to clear out. “auf und ab gehen” = to pace to and fro.

sentences.t: Er sah sich um, rechts und links, schüttelte aber zuweilen mit dem Kopf oder brummte etwas vor sich hin.
sentences.l: He looked around himself, right and left, but shook now and then with his head or grumbled something to himself.
sentences.i: He looked about him, right and left, but now and then shook his head or grumbled something under his breath.
sentences.n: German shakes ‘with the head’: “mit dem Kopf schütteln”. “vor sich hin” is the standing phrase for doing a thing to oneself and at nobody — muttering away.

sentences.t: Indem erblickte er zwei Engel, die einen Balken wegtrugen.
sentences.l: Just then he caught sight of two angels who were carrying a beam away.
sentences.i: Just then he caught sight of two angels carrying a beam away.
sentences.n: “Indem” at the head of a sentence is the older ‘meanwhile, just then’; the modern indem, ‘by doing’, is a different word altogether.

sentences.t: Es war der Balken, den einer im Auge gehabt hatte, während er nach dem Splitter in den Augen anderer suchte.
sentences.l: It was the beam that one had had in his own eye while he was looking for the splinter in the eyes of others.
sentences.i: It was the beam a man had had in his own eye while he looked for the splinter in other people’s eyes.
sentences.n: The beam and the mote of the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 7) — the tale takes the proverb at its word and has the beam carried bodily through heaven. Pfriem, naturally, does not recognize it.

sentences.t: Sie trugen aber den Balken nicht der Länge nach, sondern queer.
sentences.l: But they carried the beam not lengthwise, but crosswise.
sentences.n: “der Länge nach” — along its length; nach follows its noun in this phrase. “queer” is the 1857 spelling of quer, athwart.

sentences.t: „Hat man je einen solchen Unverstand gesehen?“ dachte Meister Pfriem; doch schwieg er und gab sich zufrieden:
sentences.l: “Has one ever seen such want of sense?” thought Master Pfriem; yet he kept silent and let himself be satisfied:
sentences.i: “Was ever such folly seen?” thought Master Pfriem; yet he held his tongue and made himself content:
sentences.n: “Unverstand” is the absence of Verstand, sense: folly rather than stupidity. “sich zufrieden geben” — to content oneself, to let a thing pass.

sentences.t: „es ist im Grunde einerlei, wie man den Balken trägt, gerade aus oder queer, wenn man nur damit durchkommt, und wahrhaftig ich sehe sie stoßen nirgend an.“
sentences.l: “at bottom it is all one how one carries the beam, straight out or crosswise, if only one gets through with it, and truly I see them knock against nothing anywhere.”
sentences.i: “At bottom it is all one how the beam is carried, straight or crosswise, so long as one gets through with it; and truly, I see them strike against nothing anywhere.”
sentences.n: “im Grunde” — at bottom, fundamentally. “anstoßen” is separable and is split right across the clause here: “ich sehe sie stoßen nirgend an”, I see them nowhere knock into anything.

sentences.t: Bald hernach erblickte er zwei Engel, welche Wasser aus einem Brunnen in ein Faß schöpften, zugleich bemerkte er, daß das Faß durchlöchert war und das Wasser von allen Seiten herauslief.
sentences.l: Soon afterwards he caught sight of two angels who were drawing water out of a well into a cask; at the same time he noticed that the cask was riddled with holes and the water ran out on all sides.
sentences.i: Soon afterwards he caught sight of two angels drawing water from a well into a cask, and noticed at the same time that the cask was full of holes and the water was running out on every side.
sentences.n: “hernach” is the old ‘afterwards’ (modern nachher). “schöpfen” is to scoop or draw water; “durchlöchert”, holed through and through.

sentences.t: Sie tränkten die Erde mit Regen.
sentences.l: They were watering the earth with rain.
sentences.n: One short sentence explains the leaking cask, and it goes straight past him: the holes are the whole purpose. “tränken” is the causative of trinken, to give a thing to drink.

sentences.t: „Alle Hagel!“ platzte er heraus, besann sich aber glücklicherweise und dachte „vielleicht ists bloßer Zeitvertreib;
sentences.l: “All hail!” he burst out, but luckily caught himself and thought “perhaps it is mere pastime;
sentences.i: “Hail and thunder!” he burst out, but luckily caught himself, and thought: “perhaps it is nothing but a pastime;
sentences.n: “Alle Hagel!” is an old oath — hail, the weather that ruins a harvest, sworn by; there is no exact English equivalent, and the rendering here keeps the weather rather than reaching for a modern curse. The literal English words happen to spell the old greeting ‘all hail’; the German is swearing by the hailstorm, not saluting anyone. “ists” = ist es; “sich besinnen” is to collect oneself, to think better of it.

sentences.t: machts einem Spaß, so kann man dergleichen unnütze Dinge thun, zumal hier im Himmel, wo man, wie ich schon bemerkt habe, doch nur faullenzt.“
sentences.l: does it give one amusement, then one can do suchlike useless things, above all here in heaven, where, as I have already noticed, one only idles anyway.
sentences.i: if it amuses a man, he may do such useless things, especially here in heaven, where, as I have already observed, one does nothing but idle.
sentences.n: “machts” = macht es, and “einem Spaß machen” is to give someone amusement. Another verb-first conditional: “machts einem Spaß, so …” = if it amuses one, then …

sentences.t: Er gieng weiter und sah einen Wagen, der in einem tiefen Loch stecken geblieben war.
sentences.l: He went further and saw a cart that had got stuck in a deep hole.
sentences.i: He went on and saw a cart that had stuck fast in a deep hole.
sentences.n: “stecken bleiben” — to stick fast; the two verbs stay together at the end of the clause.

sentences.t: „Kein Wunder,“ sprach er zu dem Mann, der dabei stand, „wer wird so unvernünftig aufladen?
sentences.l: “No wonder,” he spoke to the man who stood by, “who will load up so unreasonably?
sentences.i: “No wonder,” he said to the man standing by; “who would load up so senselessly?
sentences.n: “wer wird …?” with the future is a rhetorical scoff: who would ever do such a thing. “unvernünftig” is without Vernunft, reason.

sentences.t: was habt ihr da?“
sentences.l: what have you there?
sentences.n: Four words that set up the answer, and the answer turns the scene: he takes it for granted that the load is goods.

sentences.t: „Fromme Wünsche,“ antwortete der Mann, „ich konnte damit nicht auf den rechten Weg kommen, aber ich habe den Wagen noch glücklich herauf geschoben, und hier werden sie mich nicht stecken lassen.“
sentences.l: “Pious wishes,” answered the man, “I could not come onto the right way with them, but I have pushed the cart up here successfully after all, and here they will not let me stick fast.”
sentences.i: “Pious wishes,” answered the man. “I could not get on the right road with them, but I have pushed the cart safely up here after all, and here they will not leave me stuck.”
sentences.n: “fromme Wünsche” — pious wishes: good intentions that were never acted on, and here a cart-load of them. “glücklich” again means ‘successfully, without mishap’, not ‘happily’.

sentences.t: Wirklich kam ein Engel und spannte zwei Pferde vor.
sentences.l: Really an angel came and harnessed two horses in front.
sentences.i: Sure enough, an angel came and harnessed two horses in front.
sentences.n: “wirklich” here is ‘sure enough, and indeed’. “vorspannen” splits: spannte … vor — and it is the particle at the end that says the horses go in front.

sentences.t: „Ganz gut,“ meinte Pfriem, „aber zwei Pferde bringen den Wagen nicht heraus, viere müssen wenigstens davor.“
sentences.l: “Quite good,” remarked Pfriem, “but two horses do not bring the cart out, four at least must be in front of it.”
sentences.i: “Well and good,” said Pfriem, “but two horses will not get the cart out; there must be four in front of it at least.”
sentences.n: “meinen” here introduces speech — remarked, said — and not silent thought, though it does mean ‘to be of the opinion’. “viere” is an old inflected form of vier, four. “müssen … davor” has no verb of motion again: ‘must (go) in front of it’.

sentences.t: Ein anderer Engel kam und führte noch zwei Pferde herbei, spannte sie aber nicht vorn sondern hinten an.
sentences.l: Another angel came and led two more horses up, but harnessed them not at the front but at the back.
sentences.i: Another angel came and led up two more horses, but hitched them on at the back and not at the front.
sentences.n: A different separable verb this time: “anspannen”, spannte … an, to hitch on — where the last one had the particle vor. Everything Pfriem is about to say hangs on that difference, and on vorn and hinten.

sentences.t: Das war dem Meister Pfriem zu viel.
sentences.l: That was too much for Master Pfriem.
sentences.n: The dative “dem Meister Pfriem” marks the person for whom it is too much; English needs ‘for’ to say the same thing.

sentences.t: „Talpatsch,“ brach er los, „was machst du da?
sentences.l: “Bungler,” he broke out, “what are you doing there?
sentences.i: “Clumsy oaf,” he burst out, “what are you doing there?
sentences.n: “Talpatsch” is a borrowed word of drifting sense — from Hungarian talpas, a foot-soldier, it came to mean a clumsy lout; what exact colour it carried in 1857 is not certain, though the insult is plainly ‘blundering oaf’. Note that he says du to an angel, as he would to an apprentice.

sentences.t: hat man je, so lange die Welt steht, auf diese Weise einen Wagen herausgezogen?
sentences.l: has one ever, so long as the world stands, drawn a cart out in this way?
sentences.i: Was ever a cart pulled out that way, so long as the world has stood?
sentences.n: “so lange die Welt steht” — as long as the world stands; German keeps the present where English slips into the perfect. “auf diese Weise” = in this way, in this manner.

sentences.t: Da meinen sie aber in ihrem dünkelhaften Übermuth alles besser zu wissen.“
sentences.l: But there they think, in their conceited arrogance, to know everything better.
sentences.i: But there they are, in their conceited arrogance, thinking they know better than anyone.
sentences.n: “Übermuth” (modern Übermut) is high spirits run over into arrogance, and “dünkelhaft” belongs to der Dünkel, self-conceit. He is describing himself word for word and cannot hear it.

sentences.t: Er wollte weiter reden, aber einer von den Himmelsbewohnern hatte ihn am Kragen gepackt und schob ihn mit unwiderstehlicher Gewalt hinaus.
sentences.l: He wanted to talk on, but one of the inhabitants of heaven had seized him by the collar and pushed him out with irresistible force.
sentences.i: He would have gone on talking, but one of the dwellers in heaven had seized him by the collar and thrust him out with irresistible force.
sentences.n: “am Kragen packen” — to seize by the collar, the standard grip for putting a man out of doors. The pluperfect “hatte … gepackt” sets the grab a moment before the shove.

sentences.t: Unter der Pforte drehte der Meister noch einmal den Kopf nach dem Wagen und sah wie er von vier Flügelpferden in die Höhe gehoben ward.
sentences.l: Under the gateway the master turned his head once more toward the cart and saw how it was lifted up on high by four winged horses.
sentences.i: In the gateway the master turned his head once more toward the cart, and saw it lifted into the air by four winged horses.
sentences.n: “Unter der Pforte” — under, that is in, the gateway. His objection is answered without a word being said to him: the horses were never meant to pull along the ground. “ward” is the old past of werden, here forming the passive.

sentences.t: In diesem Augenblick erwachte Meister Pfriem.
sentences.l: In this moment Master Pfriem awoke.
sentences.i: At that moment Master Pfriem awoke.
sentences.n: The dream breaks off exactly where he has lost the argument — and he wakes up still holding his side of it.

sentences.t: „Es geht freilich im Himmel etwas anders her, als auf Erden,“ sprach er zu sich selbst, „und da läßt sich manches entschuldigen, aber wer kann geduldig mit ansehen daß man die Pferde zugleich hinten und vorn anspannt?
sentences.l: “Things do go on somewhat otherwise in heaven, to be sure, than on earth,” he spoke to himself, “and there much lets itself be excused, but who can look on patiently while they harness the horses at the back and the front at once?
sentences.i: “Things do go on rather differently in heaven than on earth, to be sure,” he said to himself, “and much may be excused there; but who can look on patiently while horses are harnessed at the back and the front at once?
sentences.n: “es geht … her” is hergehen, used of how things are done in a place. “mit ansehen” is to look on at something, to stand by and watch it happen. “läßt sich … entschuldigen” is the reflexive passive: much lets itself be excused.

sentences.t: freilich sie hatten Flügel, aber wer kann das wissen?
sentences.l: to be sure they had wings, but who can know that?
sentences.i: To be sure they had wings — but who is to know that?
sentences.n: The joke of the whole tale sits in this half-sentence: he grants the fact and keeps the complaint. “freilich” — admittedly, to be sure.

sentences.t: Es ist übrigens eine gewaltige Dummheit Pferden, die vier Beine zum Laufen haben, noch ein paar Flügel anzuheften.
sentences.l: It is besides a mighty piece of stupidity to fasten another pair of wings on horses that have four legs for running.
sentences.i: Besides, it is a monstrous folly to fasten a pair of wings on horses that have four legs to run with.
sentences.n: “anheften” — to fasten on, as one tacks a piece in place: the cobbler’s own word, now applied to the creation. “Pferden … anzuheften” is dative, to fasten on to horses.

sentences.t: Aber ich muß aufstehen, sonst machen sie mir im Haus lauter verkehrtes Zeug.
sentences.l: But I must get up, otherwise they will make nothing but wrong-headed stuff for me in the house.
sentences.i: But I must get up, or they will make nothing but a mess of things in the house.
sentences.n: “lauter” is not ‘louder’ but ‘nothing but, sheer’. The dative “mir” once more: they do it on me, to my cost.

sentences.t: Es ist nur ein Glück, daß ich nicht wirklich gestorben bin.“
sentences.l: It is only a piece of luck that I have not really died.
sentences.i: It is a good thing I did not really die.
sentences.n: The tale gives him the last word and lets it condemn him: he was put out of heaven for precisely the habit he is exercising in this sentence.

glossary.ansehen: ansehen — to look at (infinitive; ‘mit ansehen’ = to look on at, to stand by and watch)
glossary.aufgehoben: aufheben — picked up (past part.: ‘ich habe ihn nur aufgehoben’ = I only picked it up; separable auf-)
glossary.gerade: gerade — straight (‘gerade aus’ = straight ahead); elsewhere the same word means just, exactly
glossary.geselle: der Geselle — journeyman, a craftsman trained but not yet a master with a shop of his own
glossary.gesellen: der Geselle — journeymen (nom. pl.: ‘wie schlecht die Gesellen die Steine aufsetzen’)
glossary.grau: grau — grey (plain High German adjective here: ‘sein Haar grau und struppig’)
glossary.haut: hauen — hew, chop (2nd pl. present: ‘ihr haut nicht nach der Schnur’); also die Haut — skin, hide (‘die Haut weich schlägt’)
glossary.klopft: klopfen — knocks (3rd sg. present: ‘man klopft sich die Knöchel wund’ = one knocks one’s knuckles sore)
glossary.mögt: mögen — you may (2nd pl. present; ‘ihr mögt wohl Recht haben’ = you may well be right)
glossary.recht: recht — right, properly (adv.); also das Recht — right, what is right
glossary.richtete: aufrichten — put up, raised (3rd sg. past; ‘richtete … auf’, of raising a building; separable auf-)
glossary.räumen: der Raum — space, room (dat. pl.: ‘in den weiten Räumen’ = in the wide spaces)
glossary.spannt: vorspannen — harnesses in front (3rd sg. present; separable vor-)
glossary.spannte: spannen — harnessed (3rd sg. past; here with two particles: ‘spannte … vor’ = harnessed in front, ‘spannte … an’ = hitched on)
glossary.ungestüm: ungestüm — impetuous(ly), violent(ly) (adverb here: ‘so ungestüm Einlaß begehrte’)
glossary.weg: der Weg — way, road (not the adverb weg, away)
glossary.weiß: wissen — (I) know (1st sg. present: ‘ich weiß schon’); not the adjective weiß, white
glossary.wozu: wozu — for what, to what end
glossary.wünsche: der Wunsch — wishes (pl.; ‘fromme Wünsche’ = pious wishes)
